title: SLO replay - small-bucket burst/backoff experiment notes
body:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for the small-bucket burst/backoff SLO replay experiments — trying to reproduce p99 regressions seen in prod during microburst traffic patterns. This is lightweight, messy, and intended to capture configs and first-order signals for follow-up.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Replayed production-like burst (100 requests in 1s) into small batching buckets (max_batch=4, batch_timeout=6ms) across 3 nodes.
- Cold-cache runs show p99 ~ 780ms, warm-cache p99 ~ 310ms.
- Observed oscillatory latency spikes when a burst triggers many small batches concurrently (fanout effect) — likely KV cache pressure + scheduling jitter.
- Heuristics that helped in experiment: increasing batch_timeout to 12ms and enabling prefix-KV caching reduced p99 by ~40% in replay.

Environment / baseline:
- branch: inference-runtime/eviction-fix-local (PR linked above)
- image: gcr.io/redwood/inference:canary-2025-11-02-ev1
- hw: 3x A100-80GB in a small dev pool (same as prior runs)
- runtime flags: --max_batch_size=4 --batch_timeout_ms=6 --enable_kvcache=true --prefetch=false
- workload generator: local k6 script (attached at bottom) emulating bursts of 100 requests in 1s every 30s for 10 minutes.

Workload variants run:
1) cold-cache full restart between bursts (restart runtime after every burst) 
2) warm-cache continuous server for the whole run
3) increased batch_timeout to 12ms (warm)
4) enable prefix cache + increase timeout to 12ms (warm)
5) 2x node pool (warm) to check fanout effect

Key metrics (aggregated, median across 5 repeats):
- cold-cache, base (timeout=6ms): p50=48ms, p95=220ms, p99=780ms, qps during burst=2700 (peak), failure rate=0.2% (timeouts at 1.5s)
- warm-cache, base: p50=35ms, p95=150ms, p99=310ms, qps=2800, fail=0.05%
- warm, timeout=12ms: p50=34ms, p95=120ms, p99=205ms, qps similar
- warm, timeout=12ms + prefix-cache: p50=32ms, p95=95ms, p99=185ms
- 2x nodes, warm, base: p50=44ms, p95=210ms, p99=420ms (worse than single pool warm)

Observations / notes:
- Fanout effect: when bursts hit, small max_batch=4 causes many batches to be created simultaneously. Those batches contend on the GPU executor and push KV cache evictions (observed increased KV miss rate).
- Cold-cache worst-case: full kv cache rebuild and tokenizer overhead adds ~400-500ms tail. Good to quantify more precisely.
- Increasing batch_timeout gives room to aggregate more tokens into fewer batches and reduced scheduling spikes. Tradeoff: slight p50 impact in some cases (negligible here).
- 2x node pool increased cross-node variability; suggests loss of locality hurts KV cache hit rate and increases tail. For production, routing bursts to fewer-hot nodes might be beneficial.
- Observed CPU scheduler spikes on host when many small batches queue — need to capture perf top traces next.

Quick ASCII chart (p99 across variants):
[ cold-base ] 780ms  |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||
[ warm-base ] 310ms  |||||||||||||||||
[ warm+12ms ] 205ms  |||||||||||||
[ warm+12+pref ] 185ms |||||||||||
[ 2xnodes ] 420ms  |||||||||||||||||||||||

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) KV cache capacity and cross-node spread is main driver of tail in bursts. When the cache is cold or when requests spread across nodes, misses blow up p99.
2) Scheduling jitter from many tiny batches causes executor queuing spikes; combined with KV miss penalties multiplies tail.
3) Tokenizer+input processing (CPU) contributes meaningful overhead under cold/crazy concurrency.

Quick experiments to run next (concrete):
- Capture perf traces during identical warm runs (eBPF or perf) to see CPU time breakdown (tokenizer vs RPC vs scheduling). Owner: Devon.
- Repeat warm+12ms+prefix with larger kv_cache_size (double) to check hit-rate sensitivity. Owner: Ibrahim.
- Add experiment: sticky routing of bursts to a single node (route policy copy) to measure locality benefit. If p99 drops, consider burst-affinity routing.
- Run with max_batch_size=8 (same timeout) to check if slightly bigger batches help more than increasing timeout.

Unresolved questions / friction:
- How representative is k6 burst shape to real prod arrival (we have some prod traces but need to translate to generator). Linear ticket RED-8421 has prod trace snippets.
- Need to validate that increasing batch_timeout won't break latency SLOs for single-request steady traffic (A/B with 100 RPS steady).

Commands / snippets used (k6-ish pseudocode):
k6 run --vus 200 --duration 10m burst.js  # burst.js emits 100 reqs in 1s every 30s
# curl to collect runtime metrics via /metrics endpoint (Prom):
curl -s http://runtime.local:8080/metrics | grep kvcache_hit_rate

Data notes / where numbers came from:
- Numbers above are median of 5 runs but still noisy; raw CSVs saved to /tmp/noemi/slo-replay-raw-*.csv on my dev box (ask if you need them).
- I extracted percentiles with simple awk script; I can push artifacts to the linked GH gist if folks want.

Conclusions / actionable takeaways (first pass):
- For immediate mitigation: enable prefix-KV caching and tune batch_timeout to 10-15ms for bursty endpoints. This reduced p99 ~40% in our small replay. Low risk to p50.
- Medium-term: investigate routing policies to improve locality for bursts (burst-affinity) and increase KV cache size for hot endpoints.
- Further instrumentation needed: perf traces and per-node kvcache hit trajectories during bursts.

Next steps (owners):
- Devon: perf traces (due 2025-11-10)
- Ibrahim: kv_cache size sweep (due 2025-11-12)
- Me (Noemi): run batch_size=8 + larger timeout combos and collate raw CSVs (due 2025-11-13)

Rough TODO checklist:
